opus-5.5.text:
I think that's one of the deepest questions in the field right now, and I'm not sure anyone has a fully satisfying answer.

The core issue is that a cost function is always a proxy. When we train a language model on next-token prediction, we're not directly asking it to reason; we're asking it to compress and predict human text. Reasoning-like behaviour emerges because reasoning is useful for prediction, but the model is under no obligation to reason the way we do, or to stay grounded in how the world actually works. It just has to get the next token right often enough.

So for reasoning to stay aligned with the world, I think a few things need to happen. First, the training signal has to touch reality somewhere. Pure text is a shadow of the world. If a system can act, make predictions, and get feedback from an environment, whether a simulator, code that actually runs, or a proof checker, then errors have consequences. That pushes the model toward representations that track how things really are, rather than how people tend to talk about them.

Second, I'm increasingly interested in the idea that the architecture matters, not just the objective. A lot of what we see in current models looks like very sophisticated pattern matching, and sometimes that's indistinguishable from reasoning until you push slightly out of distribution and it falls apart. We may need systems that can iterate and build up a computation over time, something more like thinking, rather than producing an answer in a fixed number of steps. If the model has the machinery to check its own work and revise, the cost function can reward getting things right through a process, rather than through a lucky shortcut.

Third, I'd be a little humble about the word "aligned." Every cost function we write encodes our assumptions, and optimisation is very good at finding the gaps in them. I don't think you solve that with one perfect objective. You solve it with open-endedness, diversity, and lots of different pressures, so the system can't game any single one of them. Interestingly, that's closer to how evolution and science work: no single metric, just an ongoing process of exploration that keeps getting corrected by the world.

So my short answer is that you probably can't get there with a single static cost function on a static dataset. You need grounding, the ability to compute iteratively, and an open-ended process that keeps the model honest.

r001.rationale: The response mentions out-of-distribution failures and rewarding a process over a lucky shortcut, but does not state that judging adaptation to novelty requires examining why an answer was produced beyond checking correctness.

r002.rationale: It links optimization of a cost function to exploiting gaps and producing lucky shortcuts, rather than reliably tracking the world.

r003.rationale: It advocates open-ended exploration and correction by the world, but does not claim that how a system traverses open-ended spaces provides mechanistic confidence that its reasoning is world-aligned.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing first, because I think "trained on a cost function" is doing a lot of work in that question. Every learning system we've ever built is trained on some objective, including biological ones if you want to squint and call evolution an optimizer. So the question isn't really whether there's a cost function, it's whether the cost function has any real contact with the world or whether it's a proxy that drifts away from what we actually care about.

With next-token prediction, I think people underestimate how much world is actually in there. To predict the next token well on text written by humans, you end up having to model the thing the humans were talking about. You can't be good at predicting a physics textbook without some compressed representation of physics. So the reasoning isn't bolted on after the fact, it kind of falls out as the cheapest way to lower the loss. That's the optimistic story, and I think it's partly true.

The pessimistic story, which I also think is partly true, is that the loss only cares about the text, not about the world. So wherever the text is wrong, or where confident-sounding text is more common than correct text, the model learns that too. And then we come along with RLHF and we're not really grounding it in the world either, we're grounding it in what people like to read. That's a different thing. You can get a system that reasons very fluently and is subtly optimizing for approval rather than truth, and from the inside those are very hard to tell apart.

So my honest answer is that I don't think a single static cost function gets you there. What keeps biological reasoning aligned with the world is that the world keeps pushing back. You make a prediction, you act, reality disagrees, you update. The feedback loop is closed. Most of our current systems are trained in an open loop, on a frozen snapshot, and then deployed into a world they never actually touch during training.

That's a big part of why I've become interested in things like evolutionary and nature-inspired approaches, and in systems that keep learning rather than being trained once. Not because gradient descent is bad, it's remarkably good, but because I think the thing we're missing is less about the optimizer and more about where the signal comes from. If the signal comes from reality, from the model's beliefs being tested against consequences, then I'm much more comfortable. If the signal comes from a static dataset plus a reward model trained on human preferences, I think you can get something that looks like reasoning and is very useful, but you shouldn't be surprised when it comes apart in places where nothing ever checked it.

And I'd add one slightly uncomfortable thing, which is that I'm not sure we should expect a nice clean answer here. Humans aren't perfectly aligned with the world either. We reason with a lot of motivated bias. We just have enough feedback loops that the errors don't compound indefinitely. So maybe the realistic goal isn't a cost function that guarantees alignment with reality, it's an architecture of feedback where misalignment gets caught and corrected fast enough that it doesn't matter.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts fluent approval-seeking with truth-seeking, but does not say that judging adaptation to novelty requires examining why an answer was produced.

r002.rationale: It says a text-only loss or preference reward can drift from truth, but does not identify cost-function optimization as a source of shortcut solutions.

r003.rationale: It advocates feedback from reality and continual learning, but does not propose that a system’s traversal of open-ended spaces provides mechanistic confidence in world-aligned reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what the cost function actually rewards. You can train a system to produce an answer that looks convincing, but that’s not necessarily the same as training it to reason correctly about the world.

If you want its reasoning to stay grounded, there needs to be some feedback from reality. It makes a prediction, or takes an action, and what happens can contradict its model. Then the training process has to reward correcting that model, rather than just finding a better way to justify the original answer.

The difficult bit is that the cost function is always a proxy for what you really want. So I wouldn’t expect one cleverly chosen objective to solve the whole problem. I’d want to see whether the system’s reasoning still works when the circumstances change, whether it recognises uncertainty, and whether evidence actually changes its conclusions. That’s a much stronger test than whether it can give you a plausible explanation.

r001.rationale: The response says plausibility or correctness alone is insufficient and asks whether evidence changes the system’s conclusions, including when circumstances change.

r002.rationale: It identifies the cost function as a proxy that can reward convincing answers or better justifications instead of correct reasoning, describing a shortcut incentive.

r003.rationale: The response proposes reality-based feedback and testing under changed circumstances, but does not say that how the system traverses open-ended spaces provides mechanistic confidence in alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the cost function gives you a training signal, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you how the model is going to solve the problem. You can get very good at minimizing that cost by picking up on correlations that don’t hold outside your training data. So doing well on the objective and having an understanding that stays aligned with the world are two different things.

One way to push those closer together is to let the system make predictions and check them against what actually happens. If it has some internal model of how things work, it should be able to use that model in a new situation, make a prediction, and then revise it when it’s wrong. You want the world to keep supplying a corrective signal.

But I don’t think we have a satisfactory answer yet. Even if you train on that kind of interaction, there’s still the question of whether you’ve learned something general or just found another shortcut. That’s why testing on genuinely new situations matters so much.

r001.rationale: The response warns that a model may use shortcuts and calls for testing in new situations, but does not state that evaluation should examine why an answer was produced beyond whether it is correct.

r002.rationale: It says a model can minimize the cost by relying on correlations that fail outside the training data, identifying shortcut solutions from cost optimization.

r003.rationale: It proposes prediction, correction, and testing in new situations, but does not describe traversing open-ended spaces as a mechanism for confidence that reasoning aligns with the world.
